lessons.title: What is a share?
lessons.summary: Owning a slice of a company, and where those slices are bought and sold.

cards.title: A slice of a company
cards.body: A share is a tiny piece of ownership in a company. If a company has 1 million shares and you own 1,000, you own 0.1% of it — including 0.1% of its future profits.

cards.title: Why prices move
cards.body: A share's price is what buyers and sellers agree on right now. Good news about future profits pulls the price up; bad news pushes it down. Nobody sets the price — the market does.

cards.title: The Colombo Stock Exchange
cards.body: The CSE is Sri Lanka's marketplace for shares. You can't trade there directly: you open a CDS (Central Depository Systems) account through an SEC-licensed stockbroker, who places your orders.

cards.title: Market hours
cards.body: Regular trading runs 9:30 am – 2:30 pm, Monday to Friday, except market holidays. Orders placed outside those hours wait until the market opens.

quiz.question: You own 500 of a company's 100,000 shares. What do you own?
options: Nothing until it pays a dividend
quiz.explanation: 500 ÷ 100,000 = 0.5%. A share is ownership, not a loan or a coupon.

quiz.question: What do you need to trade on the CSE?
options: A CDS account opened through a licensed stockbroker
A licence from the Central Bank
quiz.explanation: Shares are held electronically in your CDS account, opened through an SEC-licensed broker.

quiz.question: When does regular CSE trading happen?
quiz.explanation: Regular trading is 9:30 am – 2:30 pm, Monday to Friday.

quiz.question: Who decides a share's price?
options: Buyers and sellers in the market
quiz.explanation: The price is simply the latest deal between a buyer and a seller.

lessons.title: ASPI and S&P SL20
lessons.summary: The two numbers that tell you how the whole market is doing.

cards.title: What an index is
cards.body: An index tracks the combined price of a group of shares. Instead of checking 280+ companies, you check one number to see whether the market went up or down.

cards.title: ASPI
cards.body: The All Share Price Index includes every company listed on the CSE, weighted by size. Big companies move it more than small ones.

cards.title: S&P SL20
cards.body: The S&P Sri Lanka 20 tracks 20 of the largest, most-traded companies. It shows how the market's leaders are doing.

cards.title: Using an index
cards.body: Compare your portfolio with the ASPI. If the market rose 10% and you made 4%, your picks lagged the market — even though you made money.

quiz.question: Which index includes every company listed on the CSE?
The S&P SL20 tracks…
quiz.explanation: It focuses on large, liquid companies.

quiz.question: The ASPI rose 12% this year and your shares rose 5%. What's true?
options: You made money but trailed the market
quiz.explanation: You gained 5%, but the market as a whole did better.

lessons.title: Dividends and P/E
lessons.summary: Getting paid for owning a share, and a quick way to judge if a price is high.

cards.title: Dividends
cards.body: Many companies share part of their profit with owners as a dividend, e.g. Rs 5 per share. Hold 200 shares and you receive Rs 1,000, minus 15% withholding tax.

cards.title: Dividend yield
cards.body: Yield = yearly dividend ÷ share price. A Rs 100 share paying Rs 6 a year yields 6%. A very high yield can be a warning sign that the price has fallen for a reason.

cards.title: P/E ratio
cards.body: Price ÷ earnings per share. A P/E of 10 means you pay Rs 10 for every Rs 1 of yearly profit. Lower can mean cheaper — or that investors expect profits to fall.

cards.title: Compare like with like
cards.body: Banks, telecoms and manufacturers have different typical P/Es. Compare a company with others in its own sector, not with the whole market.

quiz.question: A share costs Rs 200 and pays Rs 10 in dividends a year. What's the yield?
A P/E of 8 means…
options: You pay Rs 8 for each Rs 1 of yearly earnings

quiz.question: In the trainer, dividends are paid…
options: When you fast-forward through a payout month
quiz.explanation: Each company pays in certain months; fast-forward through them while holding to collect.

quiz.question: A share suddenly shows a 25% dividend yield. What should you think?
options: The price may have crashed for a reason; investigate
quiz.explanation: Yield rises when the price falls. Ask why it fell.

lessons.title: Diversify and think long-term
lessons.summary: Don't put all your eggs in one basket, and give investments time.

cards.title: One basket
cards.body: If all your money is in one company and it has a bad year, your whole portfolio has a bad year. Spreading across sectors means one problem doesn't sink everything.

cards.title: Different sectors
cards.body: Banks, telecoms, consumer goods and construction react differently to news. A rate cut may help banks' borrowers but squeeze their margins — owning several sectors smooths the ride.

cards.title: Long-term vs short-term
cards.body: Over days, prices jump around on news and emotion. Over years, prices tend to follow profits. Long-term investors ride out dips instead of selling at the bottom.

cards.title: Dips happen
cards.body: A 10% fall is normal for shares. Selling in panic locks in the loss. Ask: has the company changed, or just the mood?

quiz.question: Why own shares in several sectors?
options: One company's bad news hurts less
quiz.explanation: Diversification limits damage; it doesn't guarantee profit.

quiz.question: Your share fell 10% this month, but the company is unchanged. A long-term investor would most likely…
options: Hold, and review the company's fundamentals
quiz.explanation: Panic-selling locks in a temporary loss.

quiz.question: Over many years, share prices tend to follow…
quiz.explanation: Short-term noise fades; earnings matter in the long run.

lessons.title: Brokerage fees
lessons.summary: Every buy and every sell costs money. Frequent trading adds up.

cards.title: 1.12% per trade
cards.body: For trades up to Rs 100 million, the CSE's total cost is 1.12% of the value: brokerage 0.64%, CSE 0.084%, CDS 0.024%, SEC cess 0.072% and share transaction levy 0.30%.

cards.title: Buy and sell
cards.body: You pay on the way in and on the way out. A round trip costs about 2.24%, so a share must rise more than 2.24% before you break even.

cards.title: Trading too often
cards.body: Ten round trips a year cost over 22% of the money traded. That's why frequent trading usually beats only your broker, not the market.

quiz.question: You buy Rs 50,000 of shares. Roughly what fee do you pay?
How much must a share rise before a buy-then-sell breaks even?
quiz.explanation: You pay roughly 1.12% on each side.
